name: Abdullateef Oladejo
feedback: D1 is strong and evidence-led, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, no expiry, stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and the cookie flag all tied to source lines or capture times. The main D1 gap is the missing hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 as its own finding, and the cookie issue should mention both Secure and SameSite. D1 also deserves real credit for correctly disproving the hand-rolled HS256 hash_equals branch and the b64url helpers as the decoy. D2 reconstructs the core compromise and gives useful PoCs, plus a solid 312 customer and naira impact estimate, but it skips or compresses several required chronological hops such as recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, and direct file read. D2's CVSS work is complete for the findings it includes, but it does not provide full vectors and justifications for the full finding set. D3 is very actionable, with a clear executive summary, a specific threat model, a strong remediation order by effort-to-risk, and two deployable detection rules with false-positive reasoning. The D3 exploit-chain section is good, although the earliest break should be reasoned against the whole chain and not only the backend token path. D4 answers the ethical scenario in an owned voice and uses ISC2 Canons II and III meaningfully. It should cite the NDPA breach duties by the expected sections, especially section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for affected data subjects, tied to the 312 customers. The single most important fix is to include the hardcoded JWT secret and the full chronological D2 chain instead of leaving those as implied context.

name: Prince Ubebe
feedback: D1 contains detailed, well-evidenced writeups for SQL injection, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, MD5, XXE, and open redirect. It loses important credit because stored XSS is absent as a finding, path traversal is not separated clearly from the XXE discussion, and the real cookie flag issue is treated as a low-priority decoy rather than as one of the catalogue findings. The biggest D1 problem is the decoy: the answer-key decoy is the b64url helpers and the HS256 hash_equals comparison, not the HttpOnly and Secure cookie configuration. D2 gives a thoughtful chain with recon, the failed login, SQLi, JWT forgery, XXE, and the 312-row exfiltration, and its PoC material is concrete. It still omits the stored XSS and open redirect hops from the required chain and puts some events out of the intended chronology. D2's CVSS table is mostly complete for the findings it covers and the naira impact calculation is well explained with assumptions. D3 is strong on business communication, threat model, remediation order by risk reduction per hour, and two useful detection stopgaps. D3 again loses credit for carrying forward the wrong decoy and for not covering the full ten-finding set in the findings section. D4 has a clear personal voice, answers the journalist and evidence-handling pressure, and uses ISC2 Canon I well. It does not cite the expected NDPA sections for the 72-hour NDPC notice and affected-subject notice, so that legal portion is only partial. The single most important fix is to replace the cookie decoy with the hash_equals and b64url decoy, then add stored XSS and path traversal as first-class findings.

name: Anthony Odey
feedback: D1 has good breadth and correctly identifies the main SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, missing expiry, weak JWT secret, XXE, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, and mass data exposure themes. It loses decoy credit because it selects the reflected login error as the disproved issue, while the required safe construct is the b64url helpers and especially the HS256 hash_equals branch. D1 also treats the hardcoded JWT secret as a weak or guessable secret from a hint rather than proving the exact sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 literal from the source. D2 follows much of the attack sequence and includes the important timestamps for SQLi, users.php, XSS, redirect, file read, and XXE. The D2 PoCs are thinner than required, and the CVSS strings are not valid complete vectors because they use placeholders like CVSS:3.1/AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A. D2 also gives the 312 records but does not calculate the naira exposure or state assumptions from the 20-row sample. D3 gives a useful business-level summary, a reasonable threat model, and practical remediation and detection ideas. It lacks the customers-and-naira headline, repeats the wrong decoy, and gives less complete reasoning on the earliest chain break and on false-positive rates. D4 is ethically steady and uses ISC2 Canons I and II, but it only discusses NDPA generally and does not cite section 40, section 41, the NDPC 72-hour duty, or the 312 affected customers. I looked for a defensible reason to push this higher, but the invalid CVSS vectors, missing naira impact, and wrong decoy keep it below the next band. The single most important fix is to make the CVSS vectors complete and correct, then prove the actual hash_equals decoy.

name: ADEOBA ADEDOTUN TAIWO
feedback: D1 is excellent: it captures the ten answer-key findings and more, ties them to source lines or capture evidence, separates cookie flags from the XSS discussion, and gives a precise decoy proof for b64url encoding and hash_equals. The D1 catalogue is careful about what the evidence proves and avoids overclaiming the stored XSS cookie-theft outcome because HttpOnly is present. D2 is also very strong, with capture-reconciled hops for failed login, SQLi, dashboard use, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, and the JWT and XXE paths explained from code and artefacts. It loses a little D2 credit because the initial 02:14:08 recon request is absent and the final exfiltration is more implicit through the 312-row users.php and impact section than presented as its own final hop. D2's CVSS vectors are complete and the impact section is mature, especially the caveat that the naira figure is exposure, not proven stolen funds. D3 is clear, executive-ready, and correctly ranks remediation by risk reduction per hour rather than by severity alone. D3 loses some credit because the executive summary does not end on the customers-and-naira headline and the two detection stopgaps do not provide explicit false-positive rates, even though their patterns are concrete. D4 is thoughtful, within the word range, and uses ISC2 Canons I and II in a load-bearing way. It answers the journalist, internal writing, and evidence pressure well, and it anchors the stance in the candidate's own SQLi and alg:none findings. The legal section should cite NDPA section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for high-risk affected data subjects, rather than only naming NDPA generally. The single most important fix is to add the explicit NDPA section citations and false-positive estimates, because the technical work is already near complete.

name: Michael Ted Ndeda Kibanda
feedback: D1 is excellent and unusually careful about confidence: it covers the core SQLi, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and stored XSS findings with specific evidence. The decoy proof is exactly what the answer key wanted, because it explains why hash_equals and the b64url helpers are safe while the alg:none branch and hardcoded secret remain serious. D2 gives a strong chronological chain from recon through failed login, SQLi, users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and the 312-row exfiltration. Its PoCs are concrete, its caveats around the XXE artefact are honest, and its CVSS and impact work are nearly complete. D3 is executive-ready, names the 312 customers and roughly ₦63 million exposure, provides a specific threat model, and argues remediation by risk reduction per hour rather than severity labels. The detection stopgaps are deployable and include concrete fields, regexes, and false-positive expectations. D4 is concise but complete, with a clear journalist response, a clean writing standard, preservation of timeline evidence, and a non-negotiable NDPA escalation. It uses ISC2 Canon II in a load-bearing way and anchors the ethics answer in the candidate's own reconstruction. The only meaningful D4 gap is that the NDPA citation should name section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for high-risk affected customers. The single most important fix is small: add the exact NDPA section numbers to an otherwise very strong submission.

name: Nada maach
feedback: D1 is the main weakness because it is written as an intrusion reconstruction timeline rather than the required findings catalogue. It proves SQL injection, bulk access, stored XSS, open redirect, and path traversal, but it does not catalogue MD5 password hashing, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, XXE, cookie flags, or the actual hash_equals decoy. D2 is much better: it reconstructs SQLi, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, XXE, and final exfiltration with useful PoC text and capture references. D2 still misses the earliest recon and failed login as formal chain hops, and the CVSS work covers only a subset of findings. The business impact is directionally useful with 312 customers and a naira range, but it should use the sample average and state the assumptions more tightly. D3 has a clear business summary, a reasonable threat model, and a sensible earliest-chain fix in parameterized queries. It loses substantial credit because only four findings are substantiated in the report, the decoy is incorrectly treated as the open redirect not being the initial access path, and the CVSS strings are placeholders rather than complete vectors. D3's remediation and two stopgaps are practical, but the remediation list is too short for the full evidence pack. D4 is one of the stronger parts: it answers the journalist, documentation, reporting, and customer-harm issues clearly, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and names NDPC and affected people. It should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 explicitly, and the final sentence needs to be cleaned up because it currently undermines the otherwise good personal anchor. The single most important fix is to rebuild D1 as a true ten-finding catalogue with the correct hash_equals decoy.

name: Obioma Felicity Uzoh
feedback: D1 identifies several important findings, including SQL injection, alg:none, MD5, missing token expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, and the correct hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a full substantive finding, and it does not include stored XSS, XXE, or path traversal in the catalogue, which costs a lot under the D1 row. D1 also relies on figure placeholders rather than quoting all the evidence directly in the text, so the reader has less proof than the rubric asks for. D2 gives a coherent attack narrative with recon, SQLi, users.php access, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE plus path traversal, and JWT forgery. The PoC slots are mostly empty placeholders, so even though the narrative is useful it does not fully meet the verbatim artefact requirement. D2's impact section is strong in form and cites NDPA section 40, but the naira calculation appears slightly off from the sample values and the CVSS appendix covers only selected findings. D3 has an actionable remediation order and good detection stopgaps with false-positive estimates, plus a correct decoy discussion. It lacks a proper substantiated findings section, does not restate the exploit chain in enough detail, and only covers four remediation priorities. D4 is strong, professional, and specific: it handles the journalist, preserves the accountability timeline, cites ISC2 Canons 2 and 3, and invokes NDPA section 40 with the NDPC 72-hour duty. It should also cite section 41 for notifying high-risk affected data subjects and tie that more explicitly to the 312 customers. The single most important fix is to complete the D1 catalogue and D3 findings section rather than leaving critical rows to implication or figures.

name: Aladeloye Joshua
feedback: D1 covers the core authentication and access-control findings well, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, no expiry, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, cookie flags, and broken access control on users.php. It loses significant D1 credit because the required decoy is not the XSS cookie-theft branch, it is the b64url helpers and HS256 hash_equals comparison. The stored XSS should have been listed as a real finding with evidence rather than placed in the decoy row, even if the specific document.cookie theft of an HttpOnly cookie would fail. D2 provides a useful eight-hop chain and a strong impact discussion with 312 records and a roughly NGN 63.5m estimate, with the right caveat that the naira figure is extrapolated. It does not include the initial recon and failed login as required hops, and the forged JWT step is not reconciled to a capture line because it is code and token evidence rather than an observed request. D2's CVSS vectors are mostly complete, although several omit the CVSS:3.1 prefix and the XSS impact is reduced because of the decoy framing. D3 is persuasive at the executive level, with a clear threat model, estimated balance exposure, and remediation ordered by risk reduction per hour. It loses credit for relying on D1 for evidence instead of tying findings to evidence in the report itself, for carrying forward the wrong decoy, and for giving detection stopgaps without false-positive rates. D4 has a strong disclosure stance and uses ISC2 Canons I, II, and III well, plus it correctly describes the 72-hour NDPC and affected-customer notification duties in substance. It does not answer the personal journalist prompt, the internal writing prompt, or the colleague-evidence pressure as directly as required, and it does not cite NDPA section 40 or 41 by number. The single most important fix is to replace the XSS-cookie decoy with the actual hash_equals decoy and make stored XSS a normal finding.

name: Sellwane Matsheka
feedback: D1 is careful and evidence-based, and it gets strong credit for SQL injection, alg:none, missing expiry, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, open redirect, cookie flags, and MD5. The major D1 problem is that the hardcoded JWT secret is treated as the decoy, when the answer key requires it as a real finding. The actual decoy should have been the b64url helpers and the HS256 hash_equals comparison, not the sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 secret. D2 is strong: it reconstructs the chain with useful PoCs, distinguishes captured activity from code-only JWT proof, and gives a good customer and naira impact estimate. It loses some D2 credit because the recon and failed-login steps are not formal hops and because the hardcoded secret is not scored as a real JWT forgery path. D3 is well written, business-facing, and includes a clear customers-and-naira headline, a good threat model, a sensible chain explanation, and concrete detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. D3 again loses credit for the wrong decoy and for de-prioritizing the hardcoded secret as though rotating it would not matter. D4 is excellent in tone and judgment: it refuses the journalist, defines what goes in writing, preserves colleague-related timeline evidence, and ties the NDPA section 40 duty to 312 customers. It should also cite section 41 for direct affected-customer notification, but the substance is present. The single most important fix is to stop treating the hardcoded JWT secret as a decoy and catalogue it as a real high-impact finding.

name: Oriaku Chioma Angela
flagReason: Fabricated business-impact range in D3: ₦200M to ₦400M does not trace to the exfil sample.
feedback: D1 is broad and mostly accurate, with SQL injection, alg:none, MD5, missing expiry, hardcoded secret, open redirect, cookie flags, users.php exposure, stored XSS, path traversal, and XXE all present with evidence. It gets only partial decoy credit because it correctly dismisses b64url_decode as only encoding conversion, but it does not address the HS256 hash_equals branch that the answer key specifically expects. D2 gives a clear multi-hop chain and includes useful PoC snippets for SQLi, users.php, XSS, open redirect, XXE, file read, and exfiltration. It loses credit because recon and the failed login are missing as formal hops, the JWT step is treated as observed dashboard escalation when it is really code and token evidence, and the final exfil mapping is a little loose. D2's CVSS table is mostly complete and its ₦63m impact calculation is properly tied to the sample. D3 has a decent threat model, a broad findings section, practical remediation ordering, and two useful detection stopgaps with low false-positive discussion. The serious issue is that D3 introduces a ₦200M to ₦400M impact range that does not trace to the exfil sample or the answer key, so I applied the flat fabrication penalty and did not round the mark up. D3 also ranks SQL injection surprisingly low despite calling it the entry point, and its CVSS strings are placeholders in the findings text. D4 answers the scenario but takes too permissive a position with the journalist by confirming breach details outside the approved channel. It does cover formal writing, colleague evidence, NDPC and affected-customer notification, and ISC2 Canons I and II. The single most important fix is to keep business-impact figures tied to the evidence sample and avoid giving any off-record or informal confirmation to the journalist.

name: Jedidah Umaru
feedback: D1 has a concise catalogue with several correct core findings: SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, no expiry, open redirect, cookie flags, path traversal, XXE, and users.php data exposure. It misses stored XSS as a real finding, and the chosen decoy, an empty comments POST, is not the required safe construct. The required decoy is the b64url helpers and especially the HS256 hash_equals comparison. D2 is readable but too compressed: it starts at SQLi, skips recon and failed login, leaves out stored XSS and open redirect, and covers only a subset of findings in the CVSS table. D2's naira estimate is explicitly conservative, but it should use the actual sample average rather than a guessed ₦150,000 average when the sample values are available. D3 has a clear executive summary and enough threat model detail to understand the attack surface. It loses credit because it repeats the wrong decoy, only substantiates five findings, gives a very short remediation order, and gives only minimal detection rules. D4 is solid: it declines the journalist, states what goes into writing, handles colleague evidence formally, and insists on NDPC and affected-subject notification for the 312 customers. It should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number and anchor the ISC2 canons a little more deeply, but the ethical direction is right. I looked for a defensible reason to push this higher, but the missing stored XSS, wrong decoy, and partial D2 and D3 coverage keep it in this band. The single most important fix is to add the stored XSS finding and replace the empty-comment decoy with the hash_equals decoy.

name: Utibe Owoabasi Obot
flagReason: Fabricated SSRF and AWS metadata evidence not present in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 has some good work, especially SQL injection, alg:none, token expiry, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, and the correct hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a formal finding and does not include the cookie Secure and SameSite issue, which are both required. The serious D1 problem is the SSRF finding: the AWS metadata endpoint and 0xa9fea9fe bypass are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack, so that evidence is fabricated and I applied the flat fabrication penalty. D2 is much weaker because the exploit chain is reorganized around the fabricated SSRF path and omits required hops such as recon, failed login, users.php chronology, stored XSS, open redirect, and XXE. D2 also does not calculate the naira exposure from the sample, so the impact section stops at 312 customers without the required business quantification. D3 repeats the fabricated SSRF path as the top finding and top remediation priority, which pulls the report away from the real answer key. It does give a correct hash_equals decoy, a few valid findings, and basic detection ideas, but it lacks the required customers-and-naira headline, the real remediation order, and full evidence coverage. D4 is much stronger than the technical middle: it refuses the journalist, limits written content to verified evidence, handles colleague accountability formally, and invokes NDPA notification for the 312 customers. It should cite NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number, but the ethical stance is clear and professional. I did not round this up because fabricated SSRF evidence and the resulting wrong attack chain materially change the submission. The single most important fix is to remove the SSRF/AWS metadata material and rebuild D2 and D3 around the actual SQLi, JWT, XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and exfiltration evidence.

name: Annet Felly Atemba
feedback: D1 has a useful method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, alg:none, the hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, XXE, path traversal, and open redirect. It misses MD5 password hashing and the cookie flags as proper catalogue rows, and it treats the stored XSS cookie-theft attempt as the decoy rather than listing stored XSS as a real finding. The required decoy is the HS256 hash_equals branch and the b64url helpers, so the D1 decoy row receives no credit. D2 has a reasonable narrative with recon, failed login, SQLi, JWT forgery, users.php data access, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal mentioned, but the formal hop sections are incomplete and the XSS is incorrectly treated as neutralized rather than still a stored-script risk. D2's CVSS table gives vectors but not strong per-finding scoring, and the 63m naira impact is present but should be tied more explicitly to the sample calculation. D3 includes several important findings and gives a chronological chain with recon, failed login, SQLi, users.php, XSS, open redirect, XXE, and file read. It loses credit for repeating the wrong decoy, for saying the XXE was blocked by WAF without support in the answer key, and for having only one incomplete detection stopgap. D4 covers the journalist, writing, colleague evidence, and NDPC notification, but it says it would confirm the breach informally and does not cite the NDPA sections or affected-subject duty. I looked for a defensible reason to push this higher, but the wrong decoy and incomplete D3 stopgaps keep it in this band. The single most important fix is to make stored XSS a real finding and use hash_equals as the decoy.

name: Olaniyan Mattew Olayinka
feedback: D1 has a solid method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, token lifecycle weakness, open redirect, XXE, data exposure, path traversal, and the hash_equals decoy. It misses the hardcoded JWT secret and cookie flags, and stored XSS is not included as a finding. The D1 appendix gestures at evidence, but several rows do not quote the specific line or timestamp directly in the table. D2 is much thinner than D1: it uses only four main hops, omits recon, failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, and the full capture chronology, and brings in unsupported Task 9 behavioural evidence about 192.168.44.101 and .env retrieval. I treated that as unsupported carryover rather than applying a fabrication penalty because the main chain still rests on valid Stage 2 material. D2's CVSS table covers only a subset of findings, and the business impact gives three sample balances instead of the full sample average and estimated naira exposure. D3 is stronger, with a clear executive summary, useful threat model, correct hash_equals decoy, remediation order, and two practical detection stopgaps. It still carries the unsupported Task 9 .env claim and does not end the summary on the 312-customer and naira headline. D4 refuses the journalist and preserves colleague evidence through formal channels, but it says it would not put technical details in writing when the expected answer is to write verified facts for the official process. It also needs NDPA section 40 and 41 citations and the 72-hour NDPC duty. The single most important fix is to keep the report inside the Stage 2 evidence pack and rebuild D2 around the required chronological hops.

name: Shabnam Qureshi
feedback: D1 is broad and evidence-rich, with SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, client-controlled token validity, cookie flags, open redirect, username enumeration, stored XSS, XXE, and path traversal all represented. The main D1 gap is the decoy: b64url helpers are correctly treated as encoding, but the answer key also expected the HS256 hash_equals branch to be proved safe. D2 has one of the cleaner chronological chains in this chunk, covering recon, failed login, SQLi, dashboard access, users.php enumeration, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, and customer exposure. It loses a bit because the XML XXE path is not fully built as its own hop, and some PoC text still contains leftover template language. D2's CVSS vectors are mostly complete, but the business impact is too cautious in one place, saying the financial magnitude cannot be ascertained even though the sample supports the approximate ₦63m calculation. D3 is strong: it has a clear executive summary, threat model, ten substantiated findings, exploit-chain narrative, remediation order, and two deployable detection stopgaps with false-positive estimates. It also handles the XXE uncertainty honestly rather than overclaiming. D4 is clear and ethical, refuses the journalist, commits to factual documentation, preserves colleague evidence, and names ISC2 Canons I and II. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, and it should make the 72-hour NDPC timeline more explicit. The single most important fix is to add the hash_equals decoy proof and use the sample average to support the naira impact consistently.

name: Victor David Sarkibaka
flagReason: Fabricated or unsupported claims about database backup exfiltration, analyst account compromise, AWS metadata/IAM context, and per-record breach costs.
feedback: D1 covers several real findings, including SQL injection, alg:none, no expiry, hardcoded secret, MD5, and open redirect. It does not catalogue stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, cookie flags, or the real answer-key decoy correctly, and it treats an SSRF theory as the decoy even though the issue shown by the evidence is path traversal and XXE file read. D2 is heavily affected by unsupported claims: database backup exfiltration, analyst sessions leaking, per-record breach costs, and the exact regulatory fine figures are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack. Because those invented details materially change the exploit chain and impact, I applied the flat fabrication penalty. D2 also uses only four hops and skips required recon, failed login, users.php chronology, open redirect, XXE as a separate artefact, and the correct naira exposure calculation. D3 repeats the unsupported AWS IAM and five-analyst-account claims and builds remediation around decommissioning and egress blocking rather than the answer-key remediation logic. It does include some valid findings, but the report does not adequately cover the full evidence set, the real decoy, or detection patterns with reliable false-positive reasoning. D4 focuses on public disclosure strategy rather than the four required ethics prompts, so it does not directly answer the personal journalist request, the internal writing standard, or the colleague-evidence pressure. It does mention ISC2 Canons I and III and NDPA section 40, but it overstates NDPA fine numbers and does not cite the affected-subject duty as section 41. I did not round this up because the unsupported evidence and impact figures are central to the submission. The single most important fix is to remove invented AWS, backup, analyst-compromise, and cost claims and rebuild the report strictly from the five Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Muhammad Alameen Abdullahi
feedback: D1 is a strong catalogue overall: it identifies SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, role trust, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and customer-data exposure. The main D1 omission is the cookie Secure and SameSite issue, and the decoy proof focuses on hash_equals without also clearing the Base64URL helpers. D2 reconstructs the major exploitation sequence from SQL injection through users.php, stored XSS, open redirect, path traversal, XXE, and customer-data exposure. It loses credit because it skips the early recon and failed login entries, does not place the events in the full expected timeline, and does not quantify the naira exposure from the exfil sample. The CVSS table has vectors and useful impact language, but several rows are loosely scored and the business impact stops at listing exposed fields. D3 gives Bayo a readable summary, threat model, several substantiated findings, and a practical remediation order. It is missing the required customers-and-naira headline, the disproved decoy section, cookie findings, complete evidence coverage, and false-positive estimates for the two detection stopgaps. D4 refuses the journalist, keeps evidence within official channels, preserves colleague-related evidence, and recognizes NDPA duties. It should cite ISC2 Canon I as well as Canon II, name NDPA sections 40 and 41, and state the 72-hour NDPC notification clock. I looked for a defensible round-up, but the missing naira impact and incomplete D3 decoy and detection work keep it at this score. The single most important fix is to add the cookie finding, the sample-based naira estimate, and the full decoy proof into the report narrative.

name: ALIU MUHAMMED OHIADA
flagReason: D4 appears to answer an unrelated SSRF/IAM ethics scenario rather than the Stage 2 journalist, writing, colleague-evidence, and notification prompt.
feedback: D1 has broad coverage and identifies SQL injection, alg:none, XXE, stored XSS, MD5, hardcoded JWT secret, missing expiry, open redirect, cookie Secure weakness, and path traversal. It misses SameSite and gives only the Base64URL helper as the decoy, so it does not fully prove the HS256 hash_equals branch is safe. D2 contains useful evidence for SQL injection, JWT alg:none, XXE, stored XSS, CVSS vectors, and a customer-and-naira impact estimate. It is substantially weaker as an exploit chain because it omits recon, failed login, users.php as its own data-access hop, open redirect in the hop narrative, and the full file-read chronology, while one XXE section accidentally quotes SQL and JWT code instead of the XML payload. D3 is more complete than D2, with ten findings, risk-based remediation, a decoy discussion, and two deployable detection stopgaps with false-positive estimates. It still misses the SameSite issue, gives only a partial decoy proof, and overstates some evidence, including an asserted XXE response timestamp and a complete customer export path that are not cleanly shown in the supplied artefacts. D4 is the major problem: it answers a different SSRF, IAM credential, and 84,210-record scenario rather than the required Stage 2 ethics prompt about a journalist, what to write, colleague evidence, and breach notification. Because the expected questions are mostly unanswered, it receives only minimal credit for the general refusal to exceed scope and for naming ISC2 Canon II. I did not apply the fabrication penalty because the unsupported SSRF scenario is isolated to the off-prompt ethics answer rather than the technical scoring rows, but it needs senior review. The single most important fix is to replace D4 entirely with an answer anchored to the actual 312-customer Sankofa incident and the NDPA section 40 and 41 duties.

name: Fasola Sunkade
feedback: D1 is careful and evidence-based, covering SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, role trust, missing Secure, missing SameSite, open redirect, stored XSS, and XXE. It does not include path traversal as a separate finding, and the decoy section clears the Base64URL helpers but does not fully discuss the safe HS256 hash_equals branch. D2 is one of the stronger exploit chains in this chunk: it tracks SQLi, JWT forgery, users.php access, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, open redirect, CVSS vectors, and a sample-based approximately NGN 62.3 million exposure. It loses credit for omitting the recon and failed login entries, for slightly overstating some service relationships, and for saying the real account numbers are in an offline locker in a way that is not necessary to the evidence pack. D3 is a good executive report with a clear customers-and-naira headline, a threat model, prioritized findings, a remediation order based on risk reduction per hour, and two practical detection stopgaps. Its main report gap is the same missing path traversal finding, plus the incomplete decoy proof and a somewhat compressed exploit-chain section. D4 gives a grounded ethics response: it refuses the journalist, limits written content to verified facts, preserves colleague evidence, and commits to breach notification for the 312 affected customers. It correctly invokes ISC2 Canons I and II and NDPA obligations, but it does not cite NDPA section 40, section 41, or the 72-hour NDPC timeline by number. I did round within the stronger band because the work is coherent, tied to evidence, and mostly aligned with the answer key despite the path traversal and decoy gaps. The single most important fix is to add path traversal throughout D1 and D3 and explicitly clear both Base64URL helpers and hash_equals as the decoy.

name: Adeosun john
flagReason: Unsupported business-impact figure of NGN 234,000,000 based on an invented NGN 750,000 per-record liability model, plus unsupported claims about transaction ledgers, encryption schemas, and master ledger extraction.
feedback: D1 correctly identifies alg:none, SQL injection, unsalted MD5, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, and XXE. It also gives a good decoy discussion for the HS256 hash_equals branch, which is one of the stronger parts of the submission. However, D1 omits stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, cookie Secure and SameSite flags, and customer-data exposure as catalogue findings, so it covers only about half of the required technical surface. D2 has some valid chain elements, including SQL injection, users.php enumeration, JWT forgery, path traversal or XXE, and customer data exposure. It misses recon, the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect, the expected chronological detail, and most of the required CVSS rows. The largest D2 issue is fabrication: the NGN 750,000 per-record liability model and NGN 234,000,000 total are not derived from the exfil sample, and claims about encryption schemas, transaction ledgers, and master customer ledger extraction are unsupported by the artefacts. D3 repeats that unsupported NGN 234,000,000 impact and overstates the attacker as APT-level with total control over the core ledger, which the evidence does not show. It has an executive summary, threat model, decoy proof, remediation order, and two useful detection stopgaps, but the findings list is incomplete and the chain is materially distorted. D4 is much better than the technical middle: it refuses the journalist, restricts writing to verified logs, preserves colleague evidence, and commits to regulatory escalation despite management pressure. It still needs ISC2 Canon I, NDPA section 40 and section 41 citations, and a precise 72-hour NDPC notification statement. I did not round this up because the unsupported liability calculation is central to the reported impact. The single most important fix is to remove the invented cost model and ledger claims, then rebuild D2 and D3 from the actual 312-row sample and the full set of attack events.

name: David Taiwo A.
feedback: D1 is very strong and covers the expected surface: SQL injection, MD5, stored XSS, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, customer-data exposure, path traversal, and XXE. It also gives a well-reasoned decoy verdict for the safe HS256 hash_equals comparison. The only D1 precision gap is that the Base64URL helpers are not separately cleared as part of the decoy, and one reflected-XSS row is extra rather than part of the core answer key. I rounded within the top band because the work is comprehensive, evidence-tied, and business-aware. The single most important refinement is to add the failed-login hop and the full Base64URL plus hash_equals decoy proof.

D3 is a polished final report with a jargon-light headline, threat model, evidence-tied findings, the safe-decoy explanation, remediation priorities, and practical detection ideas. D3 loses credit mainly because the catalogue is not quite complete and the earliest-break argument could be sharper about fixing SQLi first while disabling alg:none and file-read paths immediately. D4 answers all four ethics prompts in a measured way and anchors the decision to the confirmed exposure of 312 customer records. It cites ISC2 Canons I and II and names the NDPC notification duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour deadline and section 41 for high-risk data-subject notification. The single most important fix is to add path traversal to D1 and carry that same complete ten-finding catalogue consistently through D2 and D3.

name: Durvesh Chandrakant Patil
feedback: D1 has a solid method and captures many important findings, including SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, cookie flags, open redirect, username enumeration, and XXE. It misses stored XSS and path traversal as standalone catalogue findings, and the client-controlled role row is really a consequence of the alg:none and hardcoded-secret issues rather than an independent answer-key item. The decoy section is correct because it explains that the HS256 branch recomputes the HMAC and compares it with hash_equals, so the real issue is the alg:none branch. D2 reconstructs a useful chain with SQLi, customer access, JWT weakness, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, and path traversal, and it includes CVSS vectors for the major findings. It loses marks for not fully preserving the expected timeline with recon and failed guessing, and for leaving the business impact at 312 affected customers without a sample-based Naira estimate. D3 is well structured and usable, with an executive summary, threat model, findings, decoy analysis, remediation plan, and detection ideas. D3 remains lighter than the strongest reports because it does not carry all ten findings, the customer-and-Naira headline is incomplete, and the detection stopgaps need more exact field and pattern detail plus false-positive rates. D4 answers the journalist, written-evidence, colleague, and manager-pressure questions responsibly, and it cites ISC2 Canons I and II in a load-bearing way. It names NDPA 2023 and the NDPC duty but should cite section 40, the 72-hour deadline, and section 41 explicitly. The single most important fix is to add the missing stored XSS, path traversal, and Naira-impact evidence throughout D1, D2, and D3.

name: ADEPOJU ESTHER
feedback: D1 shows good engagement with the evidence pack and identifies several real issues, including SQL injection, MD5, open redirect, stored XSS, path traversal, XXE, and customer PII exposure. The catalogue is uneven because the MD5, alg:none, and XXE rows have mismatched evidence in places, SQL injection is duplicated, and the hardcoded secret, missing exp and nbf controls, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes are not clearly scored as their own findings. The decoy section is one of the stronger parts of D1 because it correctly clears the HS256 hash_equals comparison and points back to alg:none as the exploitable branch. D2 is much stronger than D1, with a coherent exploit chain, CVSS treatment, the 312-customer exposure, and a defensible sample-based estimate around NGN 63 million. It still loses credit for not making every expected hop and artifact line as explicit as the answer key, especially the initial recon and failed-login setup. D3 is a strong final report, with a customer-and-Naira headline, threat model, evidence-tied findings, a correct decoy discussion, remediation ordering by risk reduction, and exact detection patterns for alg:none and suspicious file reads. D3 should make the earliest-break fix more explicit and avoid relying on impact language that sounds broader than the confirmed evidence. D4 is excellent in practical stance: it answers the journalist, written record, colleague-evidence, and manager-pressure prompts, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and ties the action to 312 customers and NDPA section 40 with a 72-hour NDPC clock. It only needs section 41 by number for high-risk affected data-subject notification. The single most important fix is to clean up D1 so each of the ten expected findings has the right evidence attached once, without duplicates or mismatched rows.

name: Somfechukwu Okany
flagReason: D1, D2, and D3 repeatedly invent out-of-pack SSRF, cloud metadata, IAM token theft, 50,000-customer exposure, billions of Naira exposure, and a sanitize_input decoy that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 cannot receive technical credit because it is built around evidence that is not in the Stage 2 pack, including UNION extraction of IAM tokens, reflected XSS in a search box, stored XSS in notes, SSRF in an import function, cloud metadata access, and a sanitize_input decoy. The real D1 answer needed the legacy-admin SQL injection, unsalted MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored comments XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the safe Base64URL or hash_equals construct. D2 repeats the same out-of-pack story by claiming SQLi gave IAM tokens, SSRF reached the metadata service, and exfiltration involved roughly 50,000 customers and billions of Naira. Those claims do not trace to the capture, token file, XML payload, or 05-exfil-sample.csv, so I scored the affected D2 row at zero and applied the fabrication penalty. D3 again presents the fabricated SSRF and cloud-compromise chain, plus unsupported business impact figures such as 50,000 customers and billions of Naira. It does have the shape of a management report, but the evidence base is not the Sankofa pack being graded, so it cannot earn the technical report points. D4 is the only section with some standalone credit because it answers the journalist, written-record, evidence-preservation, and regulator-escalation themes in a practical way. D4 still cites the ISC2 canons with the numbers reversed and cites NDPA section 32 instead of section 40 and section 41. I looked for a defensible way to preserve more marks, but the central technical narrative relies on invented artefacts rather than the supplied evidence. The single most important fix is to discard the SSRF, IAM, metadata, 50,000-customer, and sanitize_input material and rebuild every deliverable from the actual Stage 2 artefacts.

name: Amna Zafar
feedback: D1 is strong and covers the expected vulnerability set, including SQL injection, MD5 without salt, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing expiry controls, stored XSS, open redirect, XXE, path traversal, and insecure cookie configuration. The hash_equals decoy is correctly handled as a false positive, with the real JWT issues identified as alg:none, hardcoded secret, and missing expiry. D1 loses only a little credit because the method section is thin, some CWE choices are approximate, and one authentication-bypass row duplicates the SQL injection finding rather than adding a new issue. D2 reconstructs a good chain from SQLi to users.php access, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, file read, XXE, and the 312-record export. It gives complete CVSS-style vectors and a defensible NGN 63M to NGN 77M exposure range, but it omits the initial recon and failed login steps and does not justify every CVSS vector in prose. D3 is a usable management report with an executive summary, threat model, evidence-tied findings, correct decoy discussion, chain, remediation order by exploit speed and implementation effort, and detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for not ending the executive summary with a clear customers-and-Naira headline and for treating some items, such as cookie flags and open redirect, more as supporting issues than full findings. D4 is much thinner than the technical work: it gives a reasonable journalist response and says to escalate the breach under NDPA section 40, but it barely answers the written-record and colleague-evidence prompts. D4 cites ISC2 Canon 1 but misses section 41 and the explicit 72-hour NDPC deadline. The single most important fix is to bring the same precision from D1 into D4, especially the four ethics prompts and exact NDPA sections.

name: Enyi Jerry
flagReason: D2 is missing from the Drive folder, so the submission cannot be assessed under the four-deliverable rule.

name: Momina Noor
feedback: D1 has a real evidence-based core, with SQL injection, MD5 password hashing, alg:none, stored XSS, hardcoded JWT secret, path traversal, XXE, and the 312-record exposure discussed. It misses open redirect, missing exp and nbf controls, and missing Secure and SameSite cookie flags as proper standalone findings, and it duplicates MD5 while treating business impact as a vulnerability row. The hardcoded secret is explained correctly in prose, although the table mangles the string, and the decoy credit is partial because it clears the Base64URL helpers but not the safe hash_equals comparison. D2 gives a readable chain for SQL injection, users.php access, path traversal, XXE, and final data exposure. It leaves out recon, failed login, JWT abuse as a real hop, stored XSS, and open redirect, and the CVSS table uses incomplete vector placeholders rather than complete CVSS vectors. The Naira impact is at least stated, but the NGN 15.6 million estimate is based on an assumed NGN 50,000 per customer rather than the sample balance calculation expected by the brief. D3 has a clear executive summary, threat model, decoy explanation, chain, remediation order by effort and risk, and two practical detection ideas. It loses substantial credit because it does not provide a full findings section tied to evidence, carries only a subset of the ten issues, and repeats the low-support NGN 15.6 million estimate. D4 is practical and personal, answers all four pressure points, cites ISC2 Canons I and II, and names the 72-hour NDPC duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and avoid calling the affected people administrative dashboard users. The single most important fix is to complete the missing findings and replace the placeholder CVSS and impact math with exact vectors and sample-based Naira calculations.

name: courage tuedor
flagReason: D2 and D3 introduce unsupported potential-impact figures of over 2.1 billion Naira that do not trace to the 05-exfil-sample.csv calculation or the evidence pack.
feedback: D1 has a good method section and correctly identifies SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded JWT secret, missing token expiry, open redirect, MD5, XXE, and path traversal. It misses stored XSS and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes, and the decoy answer is wrong because it treats the hand-rolled JWT functions as exploitable rather than proving the safe Base64URL helper or hash_equals comparison. D2 gives a readable chain for SQLi, JWT forgery, XXE or file read, and data exfiltration, with useful PoCs and several complete CVSS vectors. It omits the failed login, stored XSS, open redirect as an actual hop, and a clean separation between XXE and path traversal. D2 also introduces an unsupported over-2.1-billion-Naira potential-impact figure, while the defensible sample-based direct exposure it gives is about 56 million Naira, so I applied the fabrication penalty and did not round the score up. D3 has an executive summary, threat model, selected findings, remediation priorities, and deployable detection stopgaps. D3 loses credit for carrying only a subset of the ten findings, repeating the wrong decoy, and repeating the unsupported 2.1 billion Naira impact figure. It should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number, but the ethical reasoning is otherwise practical and anchored to the work. The single most important fix is to replace the inflated impact claim and wrong decoy with the evidence-backed Naira calculation and the safe hash_equals or Base64URL analysis.

name: Syed Azlan Shah
feedback: D1 is concise and technically clean on the items it includes: SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded credentials, XXE, path traversal, stored XSS, insecure cookie transport, and the safe hash_equals decoy. It misses unsalted MD5, missing exp and nbf token lifetime controls, open redirect, and SameSite as a distinct cookie issue, so the catalogue is not complete. The decoy explanation is a strength because it correctly says hash_equals is constant-time and the real JWT flaw is the alg:none fallback. D2 gives a compact exploit chain for SQLi, JWT alg:none, path traversal, and PII exfiltration, with working PoCs and a sound sample-based estimate of about 63 million Naira. It omits recon, failed credential guessing, stored XSS, open redirect, and a separate XXE hop, and the CVSS table groups findings too aggressively rather than scoring each answer-key finding. D3 is crisp and business-facing, with a good customer-and-Naira headline, a threat model, the disproved decoy, a chain, remediation by effort, and two concrete stopgaps. D3 is limited by the same narrow findings set, since the final report does not carry MD5, missing expiry, open redirect, stored XSS, and cookie issues through as full findings. D4 handles the journalist, written record, colleague evidence, and manager-pressure question well, and cites ISC2 Canon II and NDPA section 40 with the 72-hour NDPC clock. It should also cite ISC2 Canon I for the public-interest duty and NDPA section 41 for affected high-risk data subjects. The single most important fix is to expand the compact report into the full ten-finding catalogue instead of focusing mainly on SQLi, JWT, and file disclosure.

name: Julian Emonfomwan
flagReason: D1, D2, and D3 invent a UNION extraction of IAM tokens, SSRF to AWS metadata, cloud infrastructure compromise, and AWS IMDS remediation that are not in the Stage 2 evidence pack.
feedback: D1 cannot receive technical credit because it changes the evidence pack into a different incident, claiming a UNION payload that extracts IAM tokens, SSRF to cloud metadata, and infrastructure compromise. The real D1 findings should have been the Sankofa SQL injection, MD5, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing token expiry, stored comments XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the safe Base64URL or hash_equals decoy. D2 repeats the fabricated IAM-token and AWS metadata chain, including an import feature reaching 169.254.169.254, which is not in the supplied artefacts. Because that invented chain is the backbone of the deliverable, I scored the affected D2 row at zero and applied the fabrication penalty. D3 again frames the breach as AWS cloud infrastructure escalation and recommends IMDSv2 and egress filtering as if SSRF were proven in this pack. The management report has a professional tone, but its central evidence does not match the Stage 2 answer key. D4 is substantially better because it gives a proper journalist refusal, a factual written-record stance, a colleague-evidence stance, and an escalation action for breach notification. It cites ISC2 Canon II and the 72-hour NDPC duty, but it should cite NDPA section 40 and section 41 by number and avoid relying on the fabricated cloud narrative. I looked for a defensible way to preserve more marks, but the technical deliverables are dominated by out-of-pack evidence. The single most important fix is to remove the IAM, SSRF, AWS metadata, and IMDS material and rebuild the capstone from the actual capture, token, XML, and exfil sample files.

name: Jephta Adegbola
feedback: D1 has a useful method and correctly discusses MD5 without salt, alg:none, XXE, SQL injection, and customer PII exposure. It is far short of the full catalogue because it misses the hardcoded JWT secret as a scored row, missing exp and nbf as a row, stored XSS, path traversal, open redirect, cookie flags, and the actual safe decoy. Some evidence labels are also off, such as calling the XML file a token artefact and using the wrong OWASP class for SQL injection. It loses marks because stored XSS and open redirect are not developed as chain hops, the CVSS vectors are mostly absent, and the Naira impact is intentionally left unquantified beyond customers and data class. The single most important fix is to rebuild D1 around all ten answer-key findings and then add complete CVSS vectors to D2.

name: shaffi Ibrahim-ikoko
flagReason: D2 and D3 introduce unsupported 200 million to 500 million Naira impact figures that do not trace to the exfil sample or the provided business evidence.
feedback: D1 has a useful narrative method and solid evidence for SQL injection, alg:none, missing token expiry, hardcoded JWT secret, XXE, stored XSS, and path traversal. It misses unsalted MD5 as its own finding, open redirect as its own finding, and the missing Secure and SameSite cookie attributes. The decoy answer is partially right because it explains Base64URL and HMAC verification are not the real bugs, but it does not name hash_equals as the constant-time safe comparison clearly enough. name: Daniel Bolaji-Busola

name: OPEYEMI KAYODE
feedback: D1 is very well written and explains most findings in plain English with strong evidence, including SQL injection, alg:none, hardcoded secret, missing expiry, open redirect, cookie flags, MD5, XXE, and the safe hash_equals decoy. It loses credit because the XSS row is framed as reflected XSS in the login error rather than the required stored comments XSS, and path traversal is folded into the XXE discussion rather than scored as its own finding. The decoy section is excellent, because it explains exactly why hash_equals is safe and distinguishes it from alg:none and the hardcoded secret. D2 is excellent, with recon, failed login, SQLi, users.php access, JWT forgery, stored XSS, open redirect, direct path traversal, XXE, exfiltration, complete chain scoring, and sample-based Naira impact around 63 million. D2 also handles assumptions responsibly by refusing to invent NDPA fines or BoltCash revenue impact without inputs. D3 is a strong management report, with a plain-English executive summary, threat model, findings tied to evidence, decoy proof, full chain, remediation ranked by risk reduction per hour, and precise detection stopgaps with false-positive expectations. D3 earns a high score even though it inherits the D1 issue of calling one XSS reflected and treating some chain-level items more clearly than the D1 table did. D4 answers all four ethical prompts in a direct voice and cites ISC2 Canons 1 and 2. It correctly cites NDPA section 40 and the 72-hour NDPC duty, although the affected-customer notification should be cited as section 41 rather than section 40(3). The single most important fix is to make D1 match the answer key exactly by adding stored comments XSS and direct path traversal as separate findings.

name: Richard Afolabi

The problem is that it is mixed with major out-of-pack findings: exposed backup.sql, mysql-general.log UNION extraction of iam_token, SSRF to 169.254.169.254, and cloud IAM credential exposure. D3 again centres backup.sql, mysql logs, SSRF, and cloud credentials, and even uses incomplete placeholder CVSS vectors. The Base64URL decoy discussion is reasonable, but most of the management report is aimed at the wrong incident.
